title: The Great Wall of China: One Wall, or Many?
description: Two hosts unpack how the Great Wall was built, how long it really is, and which famous claims about it are myths.
critical_facts: twenty-one thousand, one hundred and ninety-six kilometers
sources: UNESCO World Heritage List, The Great Wall (inscribed 1987), https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/438
State Administration of Cultural Heritage of China, 2012 survey: 21,196 km of walls
Yang, F. et al. (2010), Accounts of Chemical Research 43(6): sticky rice-lime mortar
NASA Earth Observatory, 'Great Wall of China' (2005) on visibility from orbit

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Welcome to Long Story Short, the show where we take one big subject and make it make sense. I'm Maya, and today we're talking about the Great Wall of China. With me is Daniel, who has spent far too many summers walking on it.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Guilty as charged. Hi, Maya. And I want to start with a small confession on behalf of the whole world: the Great Wall is not really one wall.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Okay, that's already a twist. What do you mean, not one wall?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: It's a network. Different Chinese states and dynasties built walls over roughly two thousand years. Some ran side by side, some were abandoned, some were rebuilt on top of older ones. What we call the Great Wall is really the whole family of them.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So who started it?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: The earliest walls go back to rival states in the seventh century BC. But the big moment comes after two hundred and twenty-one BC, when the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, unified China. He had the northern walls joined up and extended to keep out nomadic peoples from the steppe.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And those early walls, were they the stone walls we see in photos?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Not at all. Most were rammed earth. Workers packed soil, gravel and sometimes reeds into wooden frames, layer by layer, until it was as hard as rock. In the western deserts, the Han dynasty even used layers of sand and willow branches.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Then where do the famous brick walls and watchtowers come from?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: That's mostly the Ming dynasty, which ruled from thirteen sixty-eight to sixteen forty-four. The Ming rebuilt the wall in brick and stone, with thousands of watchtowers. The postcard sections near Beijing, like Badaling and Mutianyu, are Ming work.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Let's do the number everybody asks about. How long is it?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: In twenty twelve, China's cultural heritage agency finished a national survey. Counting every branch and every dynasty, it measured twenty-one thousand, one hundred and ninety-six kilometers. That's about thirteen thousand miles.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Wait, that's more than half the way around the Earth.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: It is, but remember, that's the total of many walls, not one line you could walk from end to end. The Ming wall alone is a bit under nine thousand kilometers. It runs from Shanhai Pass, where it meets the sea, to Jiayu Pass in the western desert.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: I have to ask about my favorite fact from school. You can see the Great Wall from space, right?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Sorry, Maya. It's a myth. The wall is long, but it's only a few meters wide, and it's roughly the same color as the land around it. From orbit, it's not visible from space with the naked eye. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said he looked and couldn't see it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: That hurts a little. Okay, give me a true fact that's even better.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Sticky rice. Ming builders mixed cooked sticky rice into their lime mortar. Chemists studied it in twenty ten and found that a starch from the rice makes the mortar stronger and more water resistant. Some of those walls are still standing because of it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Soup in the walls. I love it. But who actually did the building?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Soldiers, conscripted farmers and convicts, in huge numbers. The work was brutal, and many died. There's a famous folk tale about a woman named Meng Jiangnu, who wept so hard for her husband, who died on the wall, that a section of it collapsed.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And did all of this actually work? Did the wall keep invaders out?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Sometimes. It slowed raiders down, and the beacon towers could pass a warning hundreds of kilometers with smoke by day and fire by night. But walls only work with people behind them. In sixteen forty-four, the Manchu armies came through Shanhai Pass after a Ming general opened the gate to them.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So the strongest wall still has a door.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Exactly. In the end, the wall was as much about control as defense. It managed trade, collected taxes and marked the edge of the empire.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: What does the wall look like today?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: It became a World Heritage Site in nineteen eighty-seven, and a few sections are beautifully restored. But wind, rain, farming and people taking bricks home have worn much of it away. Reports suggest that around a third of the Ming wall has already disappeared.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: If someone listening wants to visit, where should they go?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: For your first visit, try Mutianyu. It's restored, it's less crowded than Badaling, and there's a toboggan ride down. If you want the wild, crumbling wall, go with a local guide, and please don't take a brick home.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So, to sum up: not one wall but many, built over two thousand years, about twenty-one thousand kilometers in total, held together in places by sticky rice, and sadly not visible from space.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: That's the Great Wall in one breath. Thanks for having me, Maya.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Thanks, Daniel. And thank you for listening to Long Story Short. See you next time.
